lines: You reported difficulties in 14 of 14 areas (Background and goals; Sustaining attention; Organization and time; Starting and finishing tasks; Forgetfulness in daily life; Restlessness and staying with one thing; Acting quickly and patience; Childhood and school years; How things changed over time; Different settings; Impact on work or study; Impact on relationships and daily life; Sleep, stress, mood, and health context; Strategies and support).
Your screening was 4/6 (original-0-6), above the threshold where further assessment may be useful.

Several reported everyday areas plus a positive screen is the kind of presentation an ADHD assessment would explore — but the same pattern can come from many other things, and this sketch is unvalidated.
Only a qualified clinician can determine what explains your experiences. Take both reports to your appointment.

statements.answer: I am here because I want to understand what has been going on my whole life, frankly. The school reports, the missed bills, the warning signs at work — I want a proper look at all of it, and to know what actually helps.
statements.question: What brings you to this assessment now, and is there anything about your background you think is relevant?

statements.answer: Honestly, staying focused is a daily battle. In meetings I will realise halfway through that I have absorbed nothing for ten minutes, and then I have to piece it together from context. It happens most days, I would say.
statements.question: Think about an ordinary day. What is it like for you to stay focused on one thing?

statements.answer: Organisation is a disaster area, and I say that with love for myself. Piles of unopened post, a desktop covered in files called 'final final v2'. I buy a new planner every January and it is abandoned by February.
statements.question: How do you find organizing your time, your tasks, or your belongings?

statements.answer: Starting things is the hardest part of my week. Bills sit on the counter for weeks until a late fee forces my hand — that has happened several times this year alone. It is not laziness, or at least it does not feel like it from the inside; it feels like wading through something.
statements.question: What kinds of tasks are hardest for you to start or finish?

statements.answer: I lose things constantly — keys, glasses, my phone while I am holding it. And appointments slip clean out of my head even when I have written them down. Last week I double-booked myself twice in three days.
statements.question: Do you ever forget appointments, obligations, or where you put things? What is that like?

statements.answer: Sitting still through a long meeting is genuinely painful. I click pens, bounce my leg, shift about — anything to discharge the fidgets. Afterwards I am wrung out from the effort of looking normal.
statements.question: When you need to sit still or stay with one thing, what is that like for you?

statements.answer: I interrupt people more than I would like — the thought arrives and it just comes straight out. Shopping is the other one: parcels arriving for things I do not remember ordering is a regular event in this house.
statements.question: How are you with waiting your turn, or holding back when you want to jump in?

statements.answer: School is actually well documented in my case — I was the dreamy kid, always staring out of the window. My old reports say things like 'capable but disorganised' and 'needs to apply herself'. My mum kept them all, bless her.
statements.question: Thinking back to childhood and school, what do you remember about yourself as a child?

statements.answer: It has been there as long as I can remember, though work is where it really bites now. I cannot pin down exactly when things got worse at work — it crept up as the jobs got more demanding, I think.
statements.question: How have these kinds of experiences changed over the years, as far as you can tell?

statements.answer: Everywhere, honestly, but with different costumes. At work it is missed deadlines, at home it is chaos and forgotten plans, socially it is zoning out mid-conversation. Same thread running through all of it.
statements.question: Are these experiences different depending on where you are — for example at home versus work or study?

statements.answer: Work has taken a real hit this year. I have had formal feedback about missed deadlines and sloppy handoffs, which stung because I am working so hard. It is the gap between the effort and the output that gets me.
statements.question: Can you describe a recent time when these experiences affected your work or studies?

statements.answer: My partner is patient but fraying, I can tell. They will tell me something important and I will have drifted off halfway, and then I have to ask them to repeat it, and I can see the look. It is corrosive in a slow way.
statements.question: How do these experiences affect the people around you, or your day-to-day life outside work?

statements.answer: Sleep is bad — my mind races at night going over the day, and then I am short on sleep and everything is harder. I know poor sleep makes it all worse, but the racing mind is there even in good weeks, so it is not the whole story.
statements.question: Are there things like sleep, stress, mood, or health that seem to make these experiences better or worse?

statements.answer: I have tried everything — apps, alarms, accountability buddies, a whiteboard the size of a door. Each one works for a week or two and then fades. The whiteboard is currently a very expensive wall decoration.
statements.question: What do you do to cope with or work around these experiences — routines, reminders, help from others?

statements.answer: If there is support or strategies that work for brains like mine, I want them. I am done white-knuckling through every week on effort alone.
statements.question: What brings you to this assessment now, and is there anything about your background you think is relevant?

statements.answer: It is worst when someone is just talking at me with slides. One on one I can mostly hold on, but put me in a room with a monologue and I am gone within minutes.
statements.question: Think about an ordinary day. What is it like for you to stay focused on one thing?

statements.answer: The planners are almost a tradition now — my partner buys me one every Christmas and we both know how it ends. I appreciate the optimism.
statements.question: How do you find organizing your time, your tasks, or your belongings?

statements.answer: The maddening bit is that once I finally start, I am usually done in twenty minutes. Weeks of dread for twenty minutes of admin. I cannot make it make sense.
statements.question: What kinds of tasks are hardest for you to start or finish?

statements.answer: The double-booking was embarrassing because both people knew each other. I had to confess I had just forgotten, twice, in one week, to overlapping friends.
statements.question: Do you ever forget appointments, obligations, or where you put things? What is that like?

statements.answer: Colleagues have commented on the pen-clicking, so now I try to fidget silently, which somehow takes even more energy. There is no winning.
statements.question: When you need to sit still or stay with one thing, what is that like for you?
